name: Regent's Park Outer Circle
description: Four laps of the Outer Circle, the flat road round Regent's Park that London riders use for early-morning training. About 18 km, shared with park traffic.

messages.text: London Zoo is beside the road here. It opened in 1828 and is the oldest scientific zoo in the world.
One lap of the Outer Circle is about four and a half kilometres.

name: Richmond Park Laps
description: Up Richmond Hill from the station, then two laps of the park road with Sawyer's Hill and Broomfield Hill on each. About 26 km, rolling.

messages.text: Richmond Park was enclosed as a deer park by Charles the First in 1637. Watch for deer crossing the road.
The park has a 20 mile an hour speed limit, and it applies to bikes too.
Broomfield Hill, the steepest climb on the park circuit.
Pembroke Lodge is on your left. From King Henry's Mound in its gardens there is a protected view of St Paul's Cathedral, about ten miles away.

name: Lee Valley & Walthamstow Marshes
description: Flat and mostly traffic-free: up the River Lee from the Olympic Park to Tottenham Hale, past the Walthamstow reservoirs and back over the marshes. About 15 km, with a few quiet streets near Tottenham Hale.

messages.text: Lee Valley VeloPark, where you start, hosted the track cycling at the London 2012 Olympics.
The reservoirs beside Coppermill Lane are Walthamstow Wetlands, opened to the public as a nature reserve in 2017.

name: Navestock & Havering-atte-Bower
description: Out of Harold Wood onto the quiet Essex lanes around South Weald and Navestock, back over the ridge at Havering-atte-Bower. About 28 km, gently rolling.

messages.text: These are the Navestock lanes, over the border in Essex.
Havering-atte-Bower is named after a royal palace that stood here from the Middle Ages.

name: Downe, Cudham & Knockholt
description: South from Bromley onto the North Downs lanes past Downe and Cudham to Knockholt, back over Rushmore Hill and Keston. About 32 km with several short, steep climbs.

messages.text: Down House, beside this road, was Charles Darwin's home for forty years. He wrote On the Origin of Species here.
Cudham. The lanes from here to Knockholt dip in and out of steep little valleys.

name: Ridge, Shenley & Elstree Lanes
description: North from High Barnet onto the Hertfordshire lanes through Ridge, Shenley, Letchmore Heath and Elstree, back via Well End and Arkley. About 33 km, rolling, with short stretches of main road leaving and re-entering Barnet.

messages.text: The Battle of Barnet was fought just north of the town in 1471, during the Wars of the Roses.
Elstree sits on Watling Street, the Roman road north out of London.

name: Lee Towpath to Hertford
description: One way up the River Lee Navigation from Tottenham Hale to Hertford, nearly all on the towpath, with a short road section around Hoddesdon. About 36 km and flat; come back by train from Hertford East.

messages.text: Stonebridge Lock. The towpath runs north from here all the way to Hertford.
You're riding through Ware. The gazebos along the river here were built in the 1700s.
Hertford, the county town of Hertfordshire. Hertford East station is a few minutes away.

name: Kingston to Ranmore & Headley
description: South-west London's classic run into the Surrey Hills: out through Claygate, Oxshott and Effingham, up to Ranmore Common, down to Westhumble, then Headley Lane and home over Epsom Downs. About 59 km, hilly in the middle.

messages.text: St Barnabas' Church on Ranmore Common was built in 1859.
Box Hill rises on your right, across the River Mole.
Epsom Downs racecourse, home of the Derby since 1780, is just ahead.

name: Ide Hill, Hever & Toys Hill
description: A long, hilly day in the Kent lanes: over the North Downs at Knockholt, up Ide Hill, down to Chiddingstone and Hever, back up Toys Hill and over Brasted Hill. About 69 km.

messages.text: Down House, beside this road, was Charles Darwin's home for forty years.
Much of Chiddingstone's Tudor village street is owned by the National Trust.
Hever Castle, the childhood home of Anne Boleyn, is close by.
The climb of Toys Hill, up through the woods of the Greensand Ridge.

name: Cuffley, Essendon & Hertford
description: North from Enfield through Crews Hill and Cuffley to Essendon, along the Cole Green Way railway path into Hertford, and back through Bayford and Broxbourne Woods. About 53 km, rolling.

messages.text: Theobalds Park Road is named after Theobalds, the palace where King James the First died in 1625.
In 1916 the German airship SL 11 was shot down over Cuffley, the first to be brought down on British soil.
The Cole Green Way follows the old railway line between Hertford and Welwyn.
Hertford, the county town of Hertfordshire.

name: Crab & Winkle Way
description: The traffic-free Crab & Winkle Way through the Blean woods to Whitstable harbour, back over quiet lanes by Chestfield, Radfall and Tyler Hill.

messages.text: This path follows the Canterbury and Whitstable Railway, opened in 1830 and one of the first passenger railways in the world.
Whitstable harbour. The town has been famous for its oysters since Roman times.

name: Viking Coastal Trail: Margate to Ramsgate
description: The Viking Coastal Trail along the Thanet seafront and clifftops past Botany Bay and Broadstairs to Ramsgate, back to Margate on quiet inland roads.

messages.text: Botany Bay, with its chalk stacks standing on the beach.
Viking Bay, Broadstairs. Charles Dickens spent many summers here.
Ramsgate is a Royal Harbour, a title granted by King George the Fourth in 1821.

name: Tonbridge to Penshurst & Chiddingstone
description: The Tudor Trail through Haysden Country Park to Penshurst, then quiet Weald lanes and the B2027 by Chiddingstone and Leigh, back along the Medway.

messages.text: Penshurst Place, home of the Sidney family since 1552.
Chiddingstone, a single street of Tudor houses owned by the National Trust.

name: Exedown, Harvel & Luddesdown Lanes
description: Along the foot of the North Downs, up the steep Exedown Road, then rolling lanes by Stansted, Harvel and the Luddesdown valley, back via Knatts Valley and down Cotman's Ash Lane.

messages.text: This road follows the line of the Pilgrims Way along the foot of the North Downs.
Exedown Road: a short, steep climb up the scarp of the North Downs starts here.

name: Romney Marsh Churches
description: Flat, open lanes across Romney Marsh linking its medieval churches: Snargate, Fairfield, Brookland, Ivychurch, St Mary in the Marsh and Newchurch.

messages.text: Fairfield church stands alone out on the marsh, often reached across the fields by a causeway.
Brookland's church of St Augustine has a wooden bell tower standing on the ground beside it.
St Mary in the Marsh. The children's author Edith Nesbit is buried in the churchyard.

name: Faversham Downs & Orchards
description: Up from Faversham into the quiet lanes and orchards of the North Downs by Eastling, Doddington, Wichling, Throwley and Selling.

messages.text: Doddington. The lanes from here climb onto the chalk of the North Downs.
Faversham is home to Shepherd Neame, which calls itself Britain's oldest brewer.

name: Canterbury & the Elham Valley
description: South from Canterbury through Bridge and Barham, down the chalk Elham Valley to Elham, back over the downs by Rhodes Minnis, Stelling Minnis and Petham.

messages.text: The Elham Valley. The Nailbourne stream along this valley only flows in wet years.
Elham, a village of old timber-framed houses gathered round its square.

name: Kent Downs: Toys Hill & Ide Hill
description: A hilly club favourite: the Darent Valley to Shoreham, up to Knockholt and down Hogtrough Hill, then the climbs of Toys Hill, Ide Hill and Star Hill.

messages.text: Toys Hill. A well near the top remembers Octavia Hill, one of the founders of the National Trust.
Shoreham, where the painter Samuel Palmer lived and worked in the 1820s and 30s.

name: Weald Hop Country: Goudhurst & Cranbrook
description: Rolling lanes through the orchards and oast houses of the Kent Weald: Brenchley, Horsmonden, hilltop Goudhurst, Cranbrook, Sissinghurst, Frittenden and Marden.

messages.text: Goudhurst, on its hilltop. The church tower looks out across the Weald.
Cranbrook's Union Mill, built in 1814, is the tallest working smock mill in England.
Sissinghurst, where Vita Sackville-West and Harold Nicolson made their famous garden.

name: White Cliffs, Deal & Sandwich
description: National Cycle Route 1 over the White Cliffs to St Margaret's, along the seafront through Walmer and Deal to the Cinque Port of Sandwich, back through Eastry, Barfrestone and Shepherdswell.

messages.text: St Margaret's at Cliffe. The South Foreland lighthouse on the cliffs was the first to be lit by electricity, in 1858.
Walmer and Deal castles were both built by Henry the Eighth around 1540 to guard this coast.
Sandwich, one of the original Cinque Ports.
Barfrestone's small Norman church is famous for its twelfth-century stone carvings.

name: Downs Link: Christ's Hospital to Shoreham
description: Mostly traffic-free along the old railway line of the Downs Link, from Christ's Hospital station through Southwater, Partridge Green, Henfield and Bramber, then beside the Adur to Shoreham station.

messages.text: The Downs Link runs 37 miles along old railway lines, joining the North Downs Way to the South Downs Way.
Bramber Castle, built by the Normans soon after 1066. Only part of the gatehouse wall still stands.

name: Cuckoo Trail: Heathfield to Polegate
description: The traffic-free Cuckoo Trail along the old railway line, gently downhill from Heathfield through Horam and Hailsham to Polegate station, with a short stretch on village lanes near Horam.

messages.text: The trail takes its name from Heathfield fair, where by tradition the first cuckoo of spring was let go.
This is the line of the old Cuckoo Line railway, which closed to passengers in the 1960s.

name: Forest Way: East Grinstead to Eridge
description: The traffic-free Forest Way along the old railway through the Medway valley below Ashdown Forest to Groombridge, then quiet lanes to Eridge station.

messages.text: The Forest Way follows the old East Grinstead to Tunbridge Wells railway, which closed in 1967.
Hartfield is just south of here. A. A. Milne lived nearby, and Ashdown Forest inspired the Hundred Acre Wood.
Groombridge Place, a moated seventeenth-century manor house.

name: Devil's Dyke & the Edburton Lanes
description: West through Portslade and Southwick to Old Shoreham, up the Adur on the Downs Link to Bramber, east under the Downs through Edburton, Fulking and Poynings, then the climb past Devil's Dyke and down Dyke Road to Hove.

messages.text: The lane now runs along the foot of the South Downs scarp through Edburton, Fulking and Poynings.
Devil's Dyke, said by the National Trust to be the longest, deepest and widest dry valley in the country.

name: Cuckmere Valley: Alfriston & Michelham
description: From Berwick station to Alfriston and along the Cuckmere, past the Long Man of Wilmington, then quiet Low Weald lanes by Arlington, Michelham Priory, Chalvington, Laughton and Ripe.

messages.text: Alfriston Clergy House was the first building the National Trust bought, in 1896.
Look up at the Downs for the Long Man of Wilmington, a figure cut into the chalk hillside.
Michelham Priory, founded in 1229, is ringed by a medieval moat.

name: Ardingly, Balcombe & Handcross
description: High Weald lanes from Haywards Heath through Lindfield and Ardingly to Balcombe, west through the woods to Handcross and Slaugham, back by Cuckfield.

messages.text: Lindfield, with its long High Street and village pond.
Handcross. Nymans, the National Trust garden, is here.

name: Low Weald Lanes: Hurstpierpoint & Twineham
description: Flat, quiet lanes north of the Downs from Hassocks through Hurstpierpoint, Albourne, Wineham and Twineham, back by Ditchling Common and Ditchling.

messages.text: Hurstpierpoint, below Wolstonbury Hill on the edge of the South Downs.
Ditchling. Ditchling Beacon, the highest point in East Sussex, is on the ridge above you.

name: London to Brighton: the Sussex Finale
description: The Sussex half of the London to Brighton ride, one way from Three Bridges station: Turners Hill, Balcombe, Cuckfield and Haywards Heath, Weald lanes to Ditchling, then the climb of Ditchling Beacon and the run down into Brighton.

messages.text: You are on the course of the London to Brighton Bike Ride, first held in 1976.
Ditchling Beacon starts here. At 248 metres it is the highest point in East Sussex.
Brighton station. Well ridden.

name: Ashdown Forest & Kidd's Hill
description: The Forest Way to Hartfield, then the climb of Kidd's Hill onto Ashdown Forest, across the open heath to Fairwarp, and back through Horsted Keynes, Ardingly and West Hoathly.

messages.text: Kidd's Hill, known to cyclists as The Wall, climbs from here up onto Ashdown Forest.
Ashdown Forest, the heathland that inspired the Hundred Acre Wood in the Winnie-the-Pooh stories.
Horsted Keynes station, on the Bluebell Railway, one of the first standard-gauge heritage railways.

name: Chichester, Harting Down & Stansted
description: Out along the traffic-free Centurion Way, over the South Downs by Chilgrove and Harting Down, back through the West Marden valley, the lanes by Rowlands Castle and Westbourne, and Funtington.

messages.text: Chichester Cathedral is the only medieval English cathedral with a separate bell tower.
The Centurion Way follows the old Chichester to Midhurst railway line.
Uppark, the National Trust house, stands on the Downs above South Harting.

name: Ripley, Wisley & Pyrford
description: A flat, easy loop on quiet lanes from Ripley through Ockham and Wisley, across the Wey Navigation at Pyrford Lock and back through Pyrford. About 16 km.

messages.text: In the 1880s and 1890s Ripley was the favourite destination of London's cycling clubs, who rode out along the Portsmouth Road.
RHS Garden Wisley, the Royal Horticultural Society's flagship garden, is off this lane.
Pyrford Lock, on the River Wey Navigation, which opened in 1653.

name: Basingstoke Canal: Woking to Ash Vale
description: One way along the Basingstoke Canal towpath from Woking to Ash Vale station, leaving the towpath for road links around Pirbright and Deepcut. About 18 km and flat; come back by train.

messages.text: The Basingstoke Canal was completed in 1794.
The Deepcut flight of fourteen locks lifts the canal through the woods here.

name: Reigate Heath, Leigh & Brockham
description: Flat, quiet Wealden lanes south-west of Reigate: out to Leigh, Brockham and Betchworth, back past Reigate Heath. About 20 km.

messages.text: Brockham, with Box Hill rising to the north.
The windmill on Reigate Heath, just north of here, has been used as a church since 1880.

name: Coldharbour & Leith Hill
description: Up Coldharbour Lane from Dorking to Leith Hill, west to Holmbury St Mary, round by Forest Green and Ockley and back through Coldharbour. About 34 km with two long climbs.

messages.text: Coldharbour Lane climbs for about five kilometres from Dorking to Coldharbour village.
Leith Hill Tower, built in 1765, stands in the woods just above this road.
Ockley sits on Stane Street, the Roman road from London to Chichester.

name: Holmbury & Pitch Hill
description: From Shere through Peaslake to Holmbury St Mary, south to Ewhurst, then up Pitch Hill and back across Winterfold and Farley Green. About 27 km, hilly.

messages.text: Holmbury Hill, above the village, is topped by an Iron Age hill fort.
The Pitch Hill climb starts here, up past Ewhurst windmill.

name: Tilford, Elstead & Crooksbury
description: Heath and river country south of Farnham: Tilford, Rushmoor and Elstead, then back over Crooksbury and past Moor Park. About 27 km, gently rolling.

messages.text: Tilford's two stone bridges over the River Wey are thought to date from the 13th century.
The ruins of Waverley Abbey, founded in 1128 as the first Cistercian abbey in England, are a short way south of here.

name: Horsley, Shere & Ranmore
description: Over the North Downs by Shere Road and Combe Lane to Shere, along the Tillingbourne valley, up Whitedown Lane to Ranmore and back via Effingham. About 27 km with two climbs, and about 1.5 km on the A25 between Gomshall and Whitedown Lane.

messages.text: Combe Lane drops off the North Downs into Shere.
Whitedown Lane: nearly three kilometres of climbing to Ranmore Common.

name: Surrey Hills Classic
description: The big Surrey Hills day from Dorking: Coldharbour Lane to Leith Hill, Holmbury, Pitch Hill, Winterfold and Shere, up Whitedown to Ranmore, then Headley Lane and down Pebblehill Road off the back of Box Hill. About 67 km with several long climbs.

messages.text: Leith Hill Tower, built in 1765, stands in the woods just above this road.
Holmbury Hill, above the village, is topped by an Iron Age hill fort.
St Barnabas' Church on Ranmore Common was built in 1859.
Box Hill, just west of here, was the climb of the London 2012 Olympic road races.

name: Titsey Hill, Woldingham & Lingfield
description: Up Titsey Hill onto the North Downs, round Tatsfield, Warlingham and Woldingham, down Gangers Hill and south through Crowhurst to Lingfield and Dormansland, back over the Kent border at Marsh Green. About 54 km.

messages.text: Titsey Hill climbs the North Downs escarpment towards Botley Hill.
Lingfield. Racecourse Road leads past Lingfield Park racecourse.
You're in Kent here, on the edge of Edenbridge.

name: Wonersh, Chiddingfold & Hascombe
description: Rolling Surrey Weald lanes from Godalming: Wonersh, Blackheath and Shamley Green, south to Dunsfold and Chiddingfold, and home over Hascombe. About 53 km, with short A-road sections in Godalming, at Bramley and near Chiddingfold.

messages.text: In 1881 Godalming became the first town in the world with a public electricity supply.
Chiddingfold was a centre of English glassmaking in the Middle Ages.
Hascombe Hill, above the village, has the remains of an Iron Age hill fort.

name: Brockenhurst Forest Tracks
description: A family loop from Brockenhurst station on the New Forest gravel cycle network and quiet forest roads: west along the old railway line, back past Wilverley, then through the Rhinefield inclosures and over Bolderford Bridge. Watch for ponies and cattle.

messages.text: This track follows the old Southampton and Dorchester Railway, nicknamed Castleman’s Corkscrew for its winding route.
The New Forest was made a royal hunting forest by William the Conqueror around 1079.

name: Red Squirrel Trail: Cowes to Sandown
description: The island’s traffic-free spine, following two old railway lines from Cowes through Newport and across the middle of the island to Sandown. Almost flat throughout.

messages.text: This path follows the old Cowes and Newport Railway, which opened in 1862.
Red squirrels still live wild on the Isle of Wight because grey squirrels never reached the island.

name: Meon Valley Trail Loop
description: North from Wickham on the Meon Valley Trail, a gentle traffic-free gravel path along the old railway, to Droxford, returning on quiet lanes through Swanmore and Shirrell Heath.

messages.text: The Meon Valley Railway opened in 1903 and closed to passengers in 1955.
In the days before D-Day in June 1944, Winston Churchill’s train was parked at Droxford station, near here.

name: New Forest Lanes from Lyndhurst
description: A classic forest road loop from Lyndhurst to Beaulieu, Brockenhurst and back through the Rhinefield and Bolderwood ornamental drives. Open heath with free-roaming animals, so ride steadily.

messages.text: Beaulieu Abbey was founded by King John in 1204 for Cistercian monks.
The tall conifers along the Rhinefield Ornamental Drive were planted in the 1850s.

name: Winchester and the Test Valley
description: West out of Winchester over Farley Mount to Kings Somborne, up the Test valley through Houghton to Stockbridge, and home over the downs by Crawley and Littleton. Rolling chalk lanes, with short main-road stretches through Kings Somborne and Stockbridge.

messages.text: The pyramid on Farley Mount is a memorial to a horse, later named Beware Chalk Pit, that survived a leap into a chalk pit in 1733.
Stockbridge sits on the River Test, a chalk stream famous for its trout fishing.

name: Isle of Wight Downs and Villages
description: From Newport past Carisbrooke Castle to Shorwell and Brighstone, over the downs to Calbourne, then back through the quiet north-west lanes and along the Cowes–Newport cycle path.

messages.text: King Charles the First was held prisoner in Carisbrooke Castle in 1647 and 1648.

name: Alresford and the Candover Valley
description: North from Alresford up the Candover valley, then east across high farmland to the Wields and back via Bighton. Quiet lanes and one easy B-road.

messages.text: Alresford is the terminus of the Watercress Line, the steam railway to Alton.

name: Round the Isle of Wight
description: The island classic: from Cowes out to Yarmouth, along the Military Road under the chalk cliffs, round the south coast to Ventnor, Sandown and Ryde, and back via Newport on the cycle path. Some busy coast road and some stiff climbs.

messages.text: Freshwater Bay. Alfred Tennyson lived nearby at Farringford for almost forty years.
The Military Road ahead was built in the 1860s to link the coastal forts.
Bembridge windmill, just inland, is the last surviving windmill on the island.

name: Watership Down and the Hampshire Highlands
description: A hilly downland loop from Kingsclere: up White Hill beside Watership Down, down the Test valley past Overton and Whitchurch, then over the high north Hampshire ridge by Faccombe and Beacon Hill.

messages.text: The ridge along here is Watership Down, the setting of Richard Adams’s 1972 novel.
Laverstoke Mill once made the paper for Bank of England banknotes, and is now the Bombay Sapphire distillery.
Beacon Hill, the Iron Age hill fort nearby, is where the fifth Earl of Carnarvon, who funded the search for Tutankhamun’s tomb, is buried.

name: Harting Down and Old Winchester Hill
description: A big South Downs loop from Petersfield: over Harting Down, through the Marden villages, to Hambledon and up Old Winchester Hill before the run home via East Meon. Lots of climbing on quiet lanes.

messages.text: H. G. Wells spent part of his youth at Uppark, the house above South Harting, where his mother was housekeeper.
Hambledon is called the cradle of cricket: its club played on nearby Broadhalfpenny Down in the 1700s.
Old Winchester Hill is crowned by an Iron Age hill fort.

name: Phoenix Trail Loop
description: Out along the traffic-free Phoenix Trail from Thame to the edge of Princes Risborough, returning under the Chiltern escarpment via Henton and Towersey. Flat; the return is on B-roads and lanes.

messages.text: The Phoenix Trail runs along the bed of the old railway between Princes Risborough and Oxford.

name: Jubilee River and Dorney
description: From Taplow along the traffic-free Jubilee River path to Eton, then back through Eton Wick and Dorney on quiet roads. Flat throughout.

messages.text: The Jubilee River is a flood relief channel, opened in 2002 to carry floodwater around Maidenhead, Windsor and Eton.
Eton College was founded by King Henry the Sixth in 1440.
Dorney Lake, just south of here, hosted the rowing at the London 2012 Olympics.

name: Oxford, Abingdon and Boars Hill
description: South from Oxford through Kennington and Radley to Abingdon, then back over Boars Hill for the view of the city and into town on the Hinksey cycle paths. One proper climb.

messages.text: Abingdon claims to be the oldest continuously inhabited town in England.
Matthew Arnold’s phrase “that sweet city with her dreaming spires” describes the view of Oxford from these hills.

name: Marlow, Turville and the Hambleden Valley
description: A Chiltern lanes loop from Marlow through Lane End and Frieth, up towards Ibstone, down to Turville and back along the Hambleden valley. Short, steep climbs and flint villages.

messages.text: Marlow’s suspension bridge was designed by William Tierney Clark, who went on to build the Chain Bridge in Budapest.
Cobstone Windmill, on the hill above Turville, appeared in the film Chitty Chitty Bang Bang.

name: Walbury Hill from Hungerford
description: From Hungerford through Kintbury and Inkpen, then the steep climb over Walbury Hill, down to Combe and round through Vernham Dean, Shalbourne and Ham. Quiet, hilly lanes on the Berkshire–Hampshire border.

messages.text: Walbury Hill, at 297 metres, is the highest point in South East England.
Along the ridge behind you stands Combe Gibbet, a replica of a gibbet first put up there in 1676.

name: Goring Gap and Streatley Hill
description: Across the Thames to Streatley and straight up Streatley Hill onto the Berkshire Downs, along quiet lanes past Aldworth, down Pangbourne Hill, then back through Whitchurch-on-Thames and the Chiltern woods above Goring.

messages.text: The Goring Gap is where the Thames cuts between the Chiltern Hills and the Berkshire Downs.
Aldworth church is known for the Aldworth Giants, a set of large medieval stone effigies.
Kenneth Grahame, author of The Wind in the Willows, spent his last years in Pangbourne.

name: Oxford to Woodstock and Islip
description: North out of Oxford through Cassington to Bladon and Woodstock beside Blenheim Palace, then across to the Cherwell and back through Bletchingdon and Islip. Short busier sections through Bladon and Woodstock.

messages.text: Winston Churchill, born at Blenheim Palace in 1874, is buried in the churchyard at Bladon.
Islip is the birthplace of King Edward the Confessor.

name: Christmas Common and Chinnor Hill
description: The Chiltern escarpment in one loop from Henley: up the Stonor valley to Christmas Common, down Watlington Hill, along the foot of the hills to Chinnor, then up Chinnor Hill to Radnage, through Stokenchurch and back past Ibstone and Turville Heath. Plenty of steep climbing, and a short main-road stretch through Stokenchurch.

messages.text: Henley Royal Regatta has been held on this stretch of the Thames since 1839.
The chalk triangle on Watlington Hill, the White Mark, was cut in 1764.
Red kites, now common over these hills, were reintroduced to the Chilterns between 1989 and 1994.

name: Lambourn Downs and the White Horse
description: A big Berkshire Downs loop from Wantage: over the downs to Farnborough and Chaddleworth, along the Lambourn valley, then back along the foot of the Ridgeway escarpment past the Uffington White Horse. Open and rolling, with a short main-road stretch at Great Shefford.

messages.text: Lambourn is one of Britain’s main centres for training racehorses.
The Uffington White Horse, on the hill above, is around three thousand years old.
King Alfred the Great was born in Wantage in 849; his statue stands in the market place.

name: Whiteleaf, Aston Hill and Wendover
description: From Princes Risborough up the Whiteleaf climb to Great Hampden, across the Chiltern plateau through Great Missenden, The Lee, Chartridge and Cholesbury, down Aston Hill to the Vale of Aylesbury, and back through Halton, Wendover and past Chequers.

messages.text: Roald Dahl lived in Great Missenden for over thirty years.
You are passing the Chequers estate, the Prime Minister’s country residence.
The Whiteleaf Cross is cut into the chalk above you; nobody knows for certain when or why.
